extracted.intended_audience: aspiring improvisers, beginner comedians and actors looking to learn improv
extracted.subtask_description: A beginner-focused guide to improvisational comedy covering core improv rules, differences between short- and long-form, what to expect in classes and shows, practice exercises, and the main benefits for actors. Designed to teach practical habits and course progression for new improvisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes, and
rubrics_metrics.description: "Yes, and." No matter what your partner says during a scene, your job is to build on that, by agreeing with ("yes") and adding to ("and") their statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use agreement and additive contribution rather than negation (avoid "no, but"). This is the most basic rule: establish and expand collaboratively rather than shutting down offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make choices / establish who, where, what
rubrics_metrics.description: Make choices. Establish three pieces of information at the top of the scene: who (the characters you’re playing), where (the setting), and what (the central "conflict" that drives the scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before "yes-ing" and "and-ing," determine the scene's basic facts so the scene has direction. A clear who/where/what helps partners build on the same reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen actively
rubrics_metrics.description: Listening is crucial in any style of acting, and it’s especially important when there’s no script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you aren't listening to your scene partner you will miss most of the scene. Active listening enables honest reactions and fuel for offers—being present is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get physical / show, don't tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Use your body and engage in the scene and the space. "Show, don’t tell." Interact with invisible props and react physically to elements the audience must imagine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mime realistic object interactions (weight, shape) to sell the scene. Physicality improves believability and gives audiences concrete anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form improv characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-form improv features spontaneous comedy with the help of preset scenarios or "games" (e.g., TV shows like Whose Line Is It Anyway?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-form relies on quick games, one-liners, and structured prompts; good for fast-paced, high-energy play and practicing quick thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-form improv characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-form improv doesn’t rely on preset games or jokey one-liners; the basic unit is a "scene" which can be two or more improvisers and may last longer to develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-form scenes may be mistaken for scripted sketch when isolated. They often use mimed props and build through callbacks and connections across multiple scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harold (long-form structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Harold is a long-form structure where separate scenes are improvised and then revisited twice more; ideally the three scenes connect in organic and unexpected ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harolds typically begin with a one-word suggestion from the audience and unfold into a 20–60-minute piece. Practice revisiting and connecting beats organically; study Del Close and Harold exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical improv class format and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Most courses are capped at 16 students and include eight three-hour sessions plus a graduation show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multiple tiers (intro/intermediate/advanced). Class size and session length are common standards in major improv hubs—use this to evaluate schools/programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory class focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory classes focus on exploring the joy of playing make-believe and drilling the basic rules of improv (like "yes, and" and basic scene-setting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners should expect games and exercises that build comfort, trust, and fundamental habits rather than complex forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate class focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate classes are where you master the basics and start to explore longer scenes and advanced forms/structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You'll work on sustaining scenes, stronger choices, and beginning to experiment with forms beyond short games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced class focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced classes cover more advanced concepts and forms (like the Harold) and prepare students for house team auditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced training emphasizes form work, long-form linking, and performance-ready skills; often required for ensemble selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: House team eligibility and unpaid performance realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Most theaters require completion of at least four courses/levels before eligibility to audition for house teams; house team performance is often recurring but usually unpaid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat house team as a development and exposure opportunity rather than reliable income—many notable alumni performed unpaid early in their careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't second-guess yourself (onstage decisiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t second-guess yourself. If you have a great idea based on an audience suggestion, take the plunge and run out to center stage—or you might miss your chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hesitation can kill opportunities. Commit to choices quickly onstage rather than overthinking in the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible (avoid rigid roadmaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be flexible. Going in with a full roadmap is a "death sentence." Be prepared to change direction depending on what your partner adds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring a nugget or impulse, not a fixed plot. Let partners’ offers reshape your trajectory; flexibility allows scenes to grow organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect to bomb (embrace failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect to bomb. There’s no improv show without jokes that fall flat; don’t get hung up—keep going and trust you’ll find the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalize failure. Resilience and continuing through bombs often lead to later successful beats in the same scene or show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate / teamwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborate. You can’t single-handedly put on a stellar improv show; learn to trust your team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize ensemble success over individual one-upmanship. Support partners’ offers and build collectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object work (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Object work: practice interacting with an object that isn’t actually on stage—mime its weight, shape, and how it feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use object work to make invisible props believable; focus on realistic details to sell actions (e.g., playing invisible guitar or chopping carrots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirror: face a partner like opposite sides of a mirror and move together, matching movements and speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builds groupthink and nonverbal listening; improves synchronicity and active attention to partners' physical cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Are You Doing? (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group miming game where one person mimes an activity; the next asks "What are you doing?" and is told a different activity to mime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices quick reimagination, adaptability, and clear physical communication between players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word at a Time (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a circle and tell a story with each person contributing one word at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises group timing, listening, and concise contribution; challenge is to maintain flow without overstepping turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes from a Hat (short-form game)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write scene topics on slips of paper, select at random, and act them out quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good for fast concept-to-performance practice and for developing quick character and situation setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Props (short-form game)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a variety of (preferably weird) props; pick one and create a mini-scene or one-liner inspired by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages inventiveness and unusual associations; useful for teaching object work and spur-of-the-moment ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helping Hands (short-form game)
rubrics_metrics.description: One player is the "face" (hands clasped), the other is the "hands" (arms puppet through), where the face narrates while the hands act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices teamwork, physical coordination, and commitment to partial-control comedic setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let's Make a Date (short-form game)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three improvisers are potential suitors with very specific personality quirks; a fourth is the contestant who must deduce their quirks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for sharpening strong, specific character choices and clear, repeatable comedic traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv prepares you for auditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv practice prepares you for auditions because casting directors can throw curveballs; improv trains quick choice-making under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors with improv experience adapt faster in unexpected audition situations and make confident choices with less prep time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv boosts your confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv helps teach confidence in performance and in the take on material, encouraging risk-taking rather than shrinking from opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training encourages leaps into risky choices and helps performers learn to trust themselves onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv forces you to be present / in the moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv practice strengthens being "in the moment"—listening to partners and reacting rather than waiting for cues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active listening and presence lead to more truthful, responsive performances; this skill transfers to both comedy and drama.
